claims.text: Integrating hBN into a high-strength ceramic or metal matrix will produce a composite with low friction across a wide temperature range.
The hBN-containing composite will have low wear across a wide temperature range.
The hBN-containing composite will largely retain the mechanical strength of the matrix.
The initial high-strength matrix has limited, temperature-sensitive self-lubricating behavior.
Incorporating a controlled volume fraction of hBN platelets creates a lamellar platelet structure within the matrix.
The lamellar structure of hBN facilitates shear during sliding.
hBN platelets slide over one another under shear.
Inter-platelet sliding of hBN produces in situ lubrication.
The matrix framework maintains the composite's overall mechanical strength while hBN supplies lubrication.
Relative to an unmodified matrix, the hBN composite will have a lower coefficient of friction under extreme-temperature conditions.
Relative to an unmodified matrix, the hBN composite will have reduced wear under extreme-temperature conditions.
An optimized hBN fraction will cause only a modest compromise in strength.
The unmodified high-strength matrix tends to exhibit higher friction at elevated temperatures.
The unmodified high-strength matrix tends to exhibit higher wear at elevated temperatures.
An hBN fraction that is too low provides insufficient lubrication.
An hBN fraction that is too high may reduce mechanical strength to an unacceptable level.
Matrix compatibility affects the balance between lubrication and strength over the tested temperature range.
